claim: A multimodal language model that follows navigation instructions in continuous 3D environments from a single forward RGB camera, trained once on the two standard instruction-navigation datasets with no extra collected data and no added 3D-geometry module, can come close to the best much heavier systems at a fraction of their GPU memory and latency, if at each step it writes out a coarse progress label and the predicted outcome of every candidate action before choosing one, and decides itself which frames to keep in a small fixed-size memory. Supported only if, on R2R-CE unseen validation scenes, its success rate is at least 4 points above every single-camera method without an added spatial module (including one trained on about 10 million extra samples) and within 3.5 points of the best method overall, which adds a 3D-geometry encoder; if its peak GPU memory is at most 55% and its per-step latency at most a third of that method's; and if, deployed unchanged on a physical robot, it reaches at least 60% success.

experiments: Build the model and its labels. Setup: Qwen3-VL 8B fine-tuned for one epoch (learning rate 1e-5, about 1,000 A100 hours) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE only, monocular RGB, actions MOVE / TURN_LEFT / TURN_RIGHT / STOP. At each step the model generates, in tagged text, a progress label (start, early, middle, late, near_goal), an outcome label for every candidate action (16 labels such as advance_to_goal, too_early, wrong_turn, over_turn), a keep/drop memory-write decision with a memory role (turn_start, turn_end, stop_evidence, goal_approach and others), then the action. All labels are derived deterministically from the expert trajectory and the next 5 expert actions, with counterfactual outcomes for non-expert actions assigned by rule rather than by rollout; the whole sequence is trained with next-token loss. Kept frames enter a FIFO memory of length 8.

Compare on the standard benchmarks. Setup: Habitat, R2R-CE and RxR-CE unseen validation splits; navigation error, oracle success, success rate and SPL, against panoramic, depth and odometry methods and single-RGB multimodal models, using numbers reported by each paper. Result: R2R-CE SR / SPL 49.7 / 45.3 against 52.8 / 49.2 for JanusVLN (adds a 3D-geometry encoder, no extra data), 49.7 / 45.5 for NaVILA (12.6 million extra samples and auxiliary modules), 47.0 for Uni-NaVid (3.6 million extra), 45.5 for StreamVLN (10 million extra, no auxiliary module) and 44.9 for Sim2Real; best panoramic method 50.0. RxR-CE SR 46.9 against 51.4 for JanusVLN, 49.3 for NaVILA, 48.7 for Uni-NaVid and 36.7 for Sim2Real.

Measure the resource cost. Setup: peak GPU memory and per-step inference time at memory lengths 4, 6, 8 and 10 on R2R-CE. Result: success rises steadily with memory length; peak GPU memory stays below 24 GB at every length and per-step time is 59 ms, against about 44.3 GB and 194 ms for JanusVLN, for about 3 points less success.

Test transfer to another task and to a real robot. Setup: (a) HM3D-OVON open-vocabulary object navigation, unseen validation subset; (b) a zsibot-L1 robot with a forward camera and an RTX 4090, 10 instructions in a workspace with visually similar objects and room entries and exits, three trials each, success if stopping within 1 m of the target. Result: (a) SR / SPL 38.0 / 26.9 against 37.1 / 19.8 for DAgRL+OD and 35.2 / 19.6 for VLFM; (b) 70% success.

Check how much the second training dataset contributes. Setup: train on R2R-CE alone instead of R2R-CE plus RxR-CE. Result: R2R-CE SR / SPL fall from 49.7 / 45.3 to 40.3 / 36.5 and navigation error rises from 5.34 to 6.61, below several baselines in the comparison.
